plain_title: When movement and coordination don't come easily
language_convention_note: 'Person with DCD' or 'dyspraxic person'; the UK community mostly uses 'dyspraxic'.
one_liner: A lifelong difference in motor coordination that makes everyday physical tasks clumsier and slower than expected.
in_simple_words: Developmental coordination disorder means the brain finds it harder to plan and control movement. Children are slower to learn to dress, use cutlery, write, ride a bike, or catch a ball, and they bump into things more. It isn't laziness or carelessness, and it isn't caused by a muscle or nerve disease. It continues into adulthood, where it can affect driving, cooking, and organization. Occupational therapy and practical strategies help a lot, and many people find their own clever workarounds.
what_it_can_feel_like: PE was humiliation twice a week. Nobody told me it had a name until I was 30.
I can give a lecture to 200 people. I cannot tie a bow or pour without spilling.
Once the OT showed him how to break tasks into steps, he stopped saying 'I'm rubbish at everything'.
common_signs: Clumsiness: dropping, spilling, bumping into things, tripping
Slow or messy handwriting, trouble with buttons, laces, cutlery
Difficulty with ball games, riding a bike, or learning new physical skills
Trouble planning and organizing tasks and movements
Present since early childhood and affecting daily life or school

myths_vs_facts.myth: Clumsy kids just need more practice.
myths_vs_facts.fact: Practice alone doesn't fix it, and repeated failure damages confidence. Targeted, task-based therapy works far better.
DCD is lifelong for most. Adults learn strategies and build on strengths, but the coordination difference remains.
It often comes with difficulties in organization, time, and sometimes speech, and it frequently overlaps with ADHD and dyslexia.

how_common.plain: About 5 to 6 in every 100 school-age children have DCD, boys more often than girls. It's one of the most common and least recognized neurodevelopmental conditions.
how_common.figure: 5–6% of children aged 5–11 (DSM-5-TR text estimate; study estimates range from under 2% to around 10%)

what_helps.plain_summary: Occupational therapy and physiotherapy using task-based approaches, which teach the specific skills a person wants to learn by breaking them into steps and practising them, have the best evidence. Accommodations at school and work, like extra time, typing instead of handwriting, and clear step-by-step instructions, make a big difference. Confidence and mental health matter, as years of 'being clumsy' can hurt self-esteem.
evidence_based_options: Task-oriented occupational therapy and physiotherapy (for example CO-OP)
School and workplace accommodations: typing, extra time, modified PE
Teaching specific daily skills step by step
Support for self-esteem and any co-occurring ADHD or anxiety
self_help_that_supports_care: Choosing physical activities you enjoy, like swimming or martial arts, over competitive team sports
Laying out clothes and tasks in order the night before
Velcro, elastic laces, and other low-tech fixes without shame
Joining the dyspraxia community online, where the tips are endless

when_to_reach_out: If a child is far behind others in physical skills, avoids drawing, writing, or sport, or is often told off for clumsiness, ask a doctor or school about an occupational therapy assessment. Adults who have always struggled this way can also be assessed.
is_not: Normal variation in sportiness isn't DCD. Coordination problems caused by cerebral palsy, muscular dystrophy, vision problems, or a brain injury are different conditions with different care.
hope_note: With the right tools and a bit of ingenuity, people with DCD do everything they set their minds to, usually in their own creative way.
strengths_and_differences: Many dyspraxic people are determined, empathetic, strategic thinkers with strong verbal skills, precisely because they've had to find other routes to things most people never think about.
in_young_people: Signs are usually visible by preschool. School is where DCD causes most trouble, through handwriting, PE, and practical lessons. Formal support plans help, and so does an explanation the child can use: 'my brain plans movement differently'.
